title: Expiry-dated memory: allocations carry leases that must be renewed
idea: Inverts 'an allocation lives until someone frees it': the allocator gives every long-lived block a lease renewed by access. Unrenewed blocks are compressed first, then paged out to flash and reported as suspected leaks with their allocation stack. Software only, on installed servers.
why: Long-running services leak or bloat 10-30% over their uptime; leases cap that growth with no hardware.

title: Swap per-GPU weight copies for an optical weight-broadcast tree
idea: Substitute storage with broadcast. Instead of every accelerator keeping its own copy of the model weights in HBM, a central weight store streams each layer's weights over a WDM optical broadcast tree, timed to the synchronized decode step, so each of N accelerators buffers only the 1-2 layers in flight in SRAM. HBM is left for KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are copied 8-64x across a serving pod. One copy plus broadcast (~1.4 TB/s for a 70B fp8 model at 20 steps/s) cuts weight-resident HBM ~Nx, freeing 50-90% of HBM in weight-dominated serving. Attacks the HBM TSV tax and capital intensity.

title: Kaleidoscope: one tensor copy, many layouts via controller remapping
idea: A kaleidoscope shows many patterns from one set of beads: the memory controller exposes row-major, column-major and tiled 'views' of a single physical tensor through programmable address swizzles, so training no longer keeps transposed weight copies, layout-converted buffers or im2col expansions.
why: Duplicate layouts and expansions take 10-30% of training memory; removing them is 1.1-1.4x capacity.

title: Rack-wide lockstep layer broadcast replaces per-server weight copies
idea: One memory sled per rack holds the model weights once. It broadcasts each layer over a multicast optical fabric while all 64 servers execute that same layer in lockstep. Each GPU keeps only a two-layer double buffer of weights. Spatial replication becomes a synchronized schedule in time.
why: Weights are replicated N times today; this makes it one copy per rack. That frees 40-80% of each GPU's HBM for KV, or allows proportionally less HBM per accelerator.

title: Photoconductive receivers let one optical broadcast replace replicated weight copies
idea: Today every GPU's HBM holds an identical weight copy for data-parallel inference. Instead, a single master copy is broadcast over waveguide or free-space optics to dozens of compute dies. Each die captures the bits just in time with photoconductive Ge sampling receivers and keeps only a small staging buffer.
why: Replication is often 4-16x the model size per cluster. Broadcast cuts that DRAM/HBM to about one copy plus buffers (facts 5, 6).

title: Xenon strobe multicast: one weight read lights up all chiplets
idea: A xenon flash lights a whole room at once; the HBM base die gets a multicast fabric so one row read of a weight tile is delivered simultaneously to every compute chiplet in the package, and to all batched tenants of the same model, replacing per-chiplet weight copies with one shared copy.
why: With 8-16 consumers per read, DRAM energy per consumed weight bit falls 8-16x, and package weight DRAM shrinks by the replica count (energy, density).

title: Compiler swaps pointer structures for succinct ones with rank/select instructions
idea: IFR: indexes sized at the information-theoretic minimum. Closest: a profile-guided compiler pass replaces read-mostly maps, sets and trees with succinct equivalents (Elias-Fano, wavelet trees, compressed tries) backed by new rank/select instructions.
why: 2-5x footprint cut for indexes and graphs in search, ads and genomics.

title: One model per person: users as 1-bit deltas over shared base
idea: From the extreme of a personalized model for every user: each fine-tune is stored as a sign-only 1-bit delta mask with per-matrix scales over one resident base and applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel, so millions of personal models share a single base in HBM.
why: A 1-bit delta is 16x smaller than BF16 weights and is never materialized; per-user model memory falls 16x+, and water with it.

title: Core-plane-sized memory sheets on display glass as cold tier
idea: Core planes were big, cheap, hand-woven panels; revive the form factor as large-area memory on glass: 2 um-rule oxide-TFT gain cells patterned on glass sheets (prototyped on 4-6 inch glass in a university nanofab) and read through edge-mounted silicon sense chips, giving ~30 GB per square metre at ~1 us.
why: Glass processing costs ~100x less per area than silicon; a microsecond cold tier shrinks DRAM to the hot set and draws on display fabs instead of DRAM fabs.

title: Z-RAM, fixed: floating-body cells for microsecond-lived activations only
idea: Z-RAM (Innovative Silicon) died because floating-body charge retention was too short and variable for 64 ms DRAM duty. Use capacitorless floating-body cells only for data whose lifetime is microseconds, such as pipelined activations between layers, so the retention spec drops ~1000x and no refresh logic is needed in a ~4F^2 SOI cell.
why: Moves activation buffers out of DRAM/HBM into on-die capacitorless cells ~5x denser than SRAM with zero refresh energy.

title: Eliminate system-prompt KV by baking fixed prompts into adapters
idea: Distill each tenant's long fixed system prompt or reference document into a tiny LoRA adapter through context distillation, so sessions carry no prefix KV at all; it ships as a software tool by a small team.
why: Prefix KV can be 10-50% of per-session memory in agent workloads; after baking, it is a few MB shared per tenant.

title: Hologram sticker: photopolymer slab stores weights read by light
idea: Credit-card holograms are cheap: record model weights as page holograms in a room-temperature-cured photopolymer slab and read millions of bits per laser flash onto a CMOS image sensor beside the accelerator, streaming weights optically instead of holding them in DRAM.
why: Volume holography could hold TBs per cm^3 for a few dollars with zero high-temperature processing; weight DRAM eliminated for read-only models if readout reaches ~100 GB/s.

title: Electrochromic rewritable optical pages host the LoRA adapter library
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a roll-to-roll coated electrochromic film (WO3/PEDOT) is written electrically through a passive printed electrode grid and read optically in parallel by an image sensor. Serving clusters park thousands of rarely used fine-tune adapters on it and load a whole adapter into HBM with one optical page read when a request arrives.
why: Multi-tenant serving keeps thousands of adapters in DRAM; a bistable optical tier that is written rarely and read in bursts frees that DRAM at film cost.

title: Swap block-compressed game textures for neural latent textures
idea: Substitute BC7 textures (8 bits per texel) with small neural latent grids plus a per-material MLP, decoded by pixel shaders on existing tensor cores at ~1-2 bits per texel in the same GDDR/HBM.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game VRAM. 4-6x compression lets GPUs ship with half the memory at equal fidelity on today's hardware.

title: 1970s SAW radar convolver computes long convolutions without buffers
idea: Revive surface-acoustic-wave convolvers from 1970s radar: on thin-film LiNbO3 or AlN, the input sequence launches as an acoustic wave past interdigital taps weighted by the filter kernel, and the summed tap output is the convolution, so neither the sliding input window nor the kernel ever sits in memory.
why: Long-convolution/SSM layers and audio/RF front ends need large sliding buffers and kernel reads; doing them in the acoustic domain removes those DRAM/SRAM buffers and their bandwidth.

title: Age polyethism assigns leaky aged chips to error-tolerant data
idea: Older worker ants take on riskier foraging jobs; recycled modules with weaker retention tails host data that tolerate rare flips (low-priority KV, activations, recomputable caches) under light ECC, while young chips hold critical state.
why: Reuse yield: turns marginal chips into useful capacity, adding 10-20% second-life supply.

title: Insurance actuary prices risk: discounted VMs with memory-pressure insurance
idea: Actuaries price rare events. A cloud or colo sells VMs 25% cheaper whose guests agree that during rare host pressure events up to 30% of their pages may be served from a compressed tier. Credits ('claims') are paid automatically per minute of measured degradation. Billing and telemetry software fits in the budget.
why: Pricing overcommit turns a hidden risk into a product, so providers can safely run 1.3-1.5x memory overcommit.

title: Drum-era optimum placement lays out weights for flash streaming
idea: Combine 1950s drum 'optimum programming' (placing data where the head will be when needed) with LLM inference from NVMe: the compiler stripes each layer's weights across all NAND channels, dies and planes in exact consumption order and double-buffers into DRAM overlays of a fixed budget so flash reads fully overlap compute.
why: Ordinary DUV-made SSDs stream weights at full internal bandwidth, so DRAM shrinks to a few layers' worth (10-50x less for batch inference).

title: Minify vector-DB residency to 1-bit codes plus flash rerank
idea: Minify every resident embedding to a binary sign code (32x smaller than FP32). Candidates are found by popcount Hamming search in DRAM and reranked with full-precision vectors fetched from NVMe.
why: Vector databases hold 32x more vectors per GB of DRAM at near-equal recall.

title: Eliminate the OS page cache: storage DMAs straight into app buffers
idea: Remove the kernel page cache entirely: file reads DMA directly from NVMe into application-owned buffers (io_uring fixed buffers), and any read caching moves into the SSD's own SLC region or a CXL-attached flash tier with a small SRAM line cache.
why: Page cache commonly holds 20-40% of server DRAM; eliminating it as a DRAM consumer frees that capacity at near-zero cost per bit.

title: Eliminate in-RAM float vectors from retrieval databases
idea: A vector database keeps only 1-bit quantized codes and graph adjacency in RAM and reranks the top candidates by reading full-precision vectors from NVMe; a small team can build it.
why: RAG vector indexes shrink 16-32x in DRAM, and these indexes are a fast-growing new DRAM demand.

title: Router-predicted MoE expert paging from existing SSDs
idea: Inverts 'all experts must be resident': only hot experts stay in DRAM. A small predictor reads router logits from earlier layers and prefetches the likely next-layer experts from NVMe RAID on existing servers, hiding flash latency behind the current layer's compute.
why: MoE models activate 5-15% of experts per token, so DRAM holds ~20-30% of the weights instead of all of them: a 3-5x cut in weight memory.

title: Transformer page-fault oracle prefetches from NVMe
idea: Worsen: let pages fault in one at a time from storage. Flip: a small sequence model trained on each application's fault traces predicts the next 1,000 pages about 200 us ahead and streams them from NVMe into a DRAM cache sized at 1% of the dataset.
why: Cost: 100x smaller DRAM for a given dataset when the learned predictor hits over 99%; trades misprediction stalls.

title: Migratory birds follow the sun: shift memory-heavy services across time zones
idea: Birds don't winter where food is scarce. A global scheduler moves memory-hungry, latency-tolerant work (batch inference, embedding refreshes, index builds, prefix-KV warmups) each day to the regions at their nightly trough. Each region's DRAM is then sized for its own interactive peak rather than the sum of all peaks.
why: Diurnal swings of 30-50% mean pooling in time cuts total provisioned DRAM 15-25% with no new hardware.

title: Eliminate the full gradient buffer by fusing backward with update
idea: Apply each layer's optimizer update the moment its gradient is computed in the backward pass, then free that gradient immediately, so the full-model gradient tensor never exists (LOMO-style fused update).
why: Removes a weight-sized buffer from training memory, about 25% of the footprint in mixed precision.

title: Shift work: co-schedule jobs whose memory peaks are anti-phase
idea: Factories run shifts so machines never sit idle. The scheduler profiles each job's memory-versus-time curve (training forward/backward peaks, batch ETL, diurnal inference load) and pairs jobs with anti-correlated peaks on a shared HBM/DRAM pool, quickly swapping out the working set of whichever partner is in its trough. Pairing is solved like a shift roster.
why: Pools sized for the sum of peaks become pools sized for the peak of the sum, using 1.3-2x fewer GB per job across a cluster.

title: Multi-port read-only shared pool for rack-wide weights and images
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: split memory into an asymmetric write-rarely class (model weights, OS images, libraries, reference data) held once per rack in a multi-ported 180 nm memory controller with 16 slow, wide ports, like 1990s dual-port VRAM or mainframe shared storage, while each server keeps only small private read-write DRAM.
why: Every server today holds its own copy of identical read-only data; removing 16 duplicates shrinks that slice ~16x, often 15-40% of server DRAM.

title: Speculative pre-free with lineage recompute on surprise reuse
idea: Invert keep-until-proven-dead: the runtime predicts each large object's last use, frees it at once, and keeps only its lineage (the operator and inputs that made it); a mispredicted later read triggers recomputation instead of a fault.
why: Peak memory of dataflow, ML and analytics pipelines drops 20-40% at a bounded recompute cost.

title: Bismuth hopper crystals: arrays stored as wavelet pyramids, read coarse first
idea: Bismuth grows as nested stair-step hopper crystals; simulation fields, images, video frames and analytics cubes are stored as integer wavelet pyramids with each level in its own pages, so previews, renders and approximate queries read only coarse levels and fetch finer levels by region on demand, while cold fine levels are dropped or sent to flash.
why: Coarse reads touch 1/16-1/64 of the bits, a >10x cut in energy per access, and dropping fine levels of cold data saves 2-4x DRAM (energy, density).

title: Starfish regrowth: compression slack pays for erasure-coded memory
idea: A starfish regrows from one arm; pages are compressed and the freed space holds erasure-code parity striped across modules, so any single module can be hot-pulled for repair and rebuilt from the rest with no net capacity cost.
why: Repair without downtime or overprovisioning; makes cheaper, less reliable recycled modules safe to deploy.

title: 2050 engineer: KV cache stored as per-sequence implicit neural field
idea: A 2050 engineer stores functions, not tables. For each long sequence, a tiny sinusoidal MLP per layer is fitted online to map (position, head) to the K/V vector and refitted incrementally every few hundred tokens, and attention queries this field instead of a table. Exact KV is kept only for the recent window and for outlier tokens the field reconstructs poorly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory. A 20-50x fit on older tokens would turn 1M-token contexts from hundreds of GB into a few GB. The accuracy risk is high.

title: Spherical-coordinate quantization of keys and embeddings
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: convert key and embedding vectors from Cartesian to recursive polar form (one norm plus d-1 angles); after a random rotation the angles are tightly concentrated, so they quantize to 2-3 bits with no per-block scale or zero-point metadata.
why: Removes quantization metadata and outlier handling; ~4-6x KV/embedding compression vs FP16 at near-lossless attention fidelity.

title: Magnetosome-chain ordering aligns embedding rows for delta compression
idea: As magnetotactic bacteria align magnetosomes into a chain along the field, a one-time pass sorts embedding-table rows along a learned principal axis or space-filling curve so neighbors are similar, then stores each row as an entropy-coded delta from its predecessor; a small index maps original IDs to chain positions.
why: Recommendation embeddings occupy terabytes of DRAM; 2-4x compression decodable at line rate.

title: Console streaming discipline: DRAM as a compiled ring window
idea: From game consoles that stream open worlds from SSD through fixed RAM: an ahead-of-time compiler profiles a workload's deterministic access order (inference layers, ETL stages, simulation sweeps) and emits a streaming schedule so DRAM is only a ring buffer refilled from parallel NVMe at exactly the needed rate.
why: For deterministic workloads only the in-flight window needs DRAM: 10-50x less DRAM with bandwidth supplied by striped SSDs.

title: Compiler lifetime typing parks short-lived buffers in refresh-free banks
idea: Arrhenius scaling puts DRAM tail retention at 125 C around 8-16 ms. The compiler tags every buffer with its lifetime (activations, per-step KV, DMA staging). Buffers whose producer-consumer gap is under 2 ms go to banks with refresh disabled, and long-lived data goes to robust NVM. On-die canary cells re-check the retention model at every boot over the 10-year life.
why: At 125 C, refresh would eat 20-40% of bandwidth. Turning it off for ~70% of banks recovers that bandwidth, so a smaller DRAM serves the same workload.

title: Real-time memory exchange fused with VM balloon drivers
idea: Combine spot-market pricing with hypervisor ballooning: tenants post idle guest memory as sell orders, the balloon driver reclaims it within seconds when bought, and the buyer receives it through a CXL pool or same-host remapping.
why: Cloud memory utilization often sits under 50%; trading idle gigabytes raises effective supply 20-30% with no new silicon.

title: Fuse the optimizer into backward so gradients never fully exist
idea: Rearrange the training step from backward-then-update to update-during-backward: the optimizer applies each parameter tensor's gradient the moment it is produced and frees it at once, with gradient clipping taken from a running norm of the previous step.
why: Removes the full gradient buffer (the size of the model): 25-40% lower training memory on existing GPUs, with no new gas-dependent DRAM output.

title: Differential-analyzer integrators hold sequence state instead of KV cache
idea: Revive analog computers, where state lived as voltage on integrators: state-space or linear-recurrent layers run on arrays of switched-capacitor integrators whose capacitor voltages are the recurrent state, updated per token and digitized only at layer outputs. Context length no longer grows memory.
why: For SSM/hybrid models a fixed few hundred KB of analog state per sequence replaces a KV cache that reaches tens of GB at 1M tokens, and state read/write energy disappears.

title: Page-aligned content-defined packaging so kernel dedup actually hits
idea: Box: dedup enablement × build and packaging toolchain × 4 KB/2 MB chunk × build time × content-defined chunking with alignment padding. Binaries, container layers and model files are laid out so identical content lands on identical page boundaries across versions and tenants, letting existing same-page merging match it.
why: Small offsets defeat page dedup today; alignment lifts merge rates from a few percent to 20–40% on dense hosts, a pure toolchain change free of fluorinated chemistry.

title: Fiducial marks: pilot-calibrated two-bit-per-cell DRAM with soft decoding
idea: Pick-and-place machines read fiducial marks to correct for drift. Each DRAM page embeds pilot cells with known values, read through the sense amp at several reference levels to track drift and leakage. That lets each cell hold 2 bits (4 charge levels), and a soft-decision LDPC decoder uses pilot-calibrated likelihoods to turn a ~1% raw symbol error rate into reliable reads for a compressed or cold tier.
why: Doubles the bits per capacitor, giving 2x density on the same wafer area and EUV layers for page-granularity tiers where LDPC latency is hidden; the 1% error budget is what makes multi-level DRAM viable.

title: Byte-rent compiler: auto-narrow every field to its observed range
idea: Po: programs pay rent for every byte per second. A profile-guided compiler pass records production value ranges and cardinalities, then recompiles structs with the narrowest integer widths, enums as bitfields and packed booleans, with guarded widening on overflow.
why: Typical business objects store 8-16-bit values in 64-bit fields; auto-narrowing cuts object footprint 30-50%.

title: Apoptotic eat-me telemetry retires memory packages before they fail
idea: Like cells displaying phosphatidylserine before apoptosis, each DRAM package exports correctable-error rate, retention drift and hammer-count signals; crossing a threshold triggers live migration of its pages and schedules a tool-less swap of just that unit, so failures never crash jobs or force whole-board scrap.
why: Repairability: removes ~10% just-in-case DRAM headroom and extends module life 2-3x, cutting replacement demand.

title: HFT zero-copy ownership: one physical buffer for the whole stack
idea: From high-frequency traders who never copy a packet: NIC, kernel, application and GPU pass capabilities to one physical buffer through IOMMU-enforced ownership transfer (move semantics in hardware), abolishing socket buffers, page-cache copies and GPU staging buffers.
why: Data is often held 3-5 times across the I/O stack; single-copy cuts I/O buffer DRAM 3-5x and the copy energy (fact 5).

title: Kanban buffers: memory scales with throughput, not connection count
idea: Toyota kanban caps work in process with physical cards. Per-connection pinned send and receive buffers (RDMA queue pairs, TCP socket buffers, gRPC channels) are replaced by a fixed pool of buffer 'cards' sized by Little's law: throughput times latency times a safety factor. A sender must hold a card (a credit) to transmit, and cards return to the pool when the data is consumed.
why: Servers with 10k-100k connections pin tens of GB in mostly idle buffers; kanban sizing cuts network and IO buffer memory 10-100x at the same throughput.

title: Attention computed directly on product-quantized keys
idea: Imposed limit: keys may never be decompressed. Keys are stored as 8-byte product-quantization codes; each query precomputes a small SRAM table of sub-vector dot products and scores every key with table lookups and adds, the way ANN search engines do, and fetches full values only for the top-scoring tokens.
why: Key storage shrinks 8-16x and only the top-k values are read; long-context KV footprint and traffic fall ~4-8x.

title: Run cache-sized services on gigabyte-LLC CPUs with minimal DIMMs
idea: Box: substitute × existing large-L3 CPUs (~1 GB stacked SRAM) × whole working set × deployment time × minimal DIMM population. Routers, rate limiters, feature-flag and session services whose working sets fit in ~1 GB are pinned to large-cache parts already in the fleet, with one small DIMM per channel.
why: Those services get 256–512 GB per box by default; running them cache-resident frees 80–95% of their DRAM using installed silicon, so nothing new passes through fluorinated etch or PFAS lithography.

title: KV cache whose precision decays with token age and attention
idea: Box: approximate × KV manager × 16-token block × age-triggered × format ladder FP16→FP8→INT4→INT2→evict. A background re-quantizer demotes blocks as they age and as their accumulated attention mass stays low, while sink tokens and recently attended blocks stay at full precision.
why: Attention mass concentrates on recent and a few anchor tokens; an average of 3–4 bits per value instead of 16 shrinks long-context KV 4–5×.

title: Watercolor wash: printed analog crossbar on glass computes edge weights
idea: Watercolour is painted at room temperature: solution-process perovskite or organic memristor crossbars (<150 C) on glass, program model weights as conductances and compute matrix-vector products in place for small edge models, so devices ship with no DRAM for weights.
why: Edge/IoT inference drops DRAM entirely; panel-scale low-temperature processing gives very low capex and is US-buildable.

title: Seashell spiral: logarithmically spaced KV retention with merged summaries
idea: Nautilus chambers grow geometrically: keep every token of the last 256, every 2nd from 256-1k, every 4th from 1k-4k and so on, folding dropped tokens' KV into their surviving neighbour by attention-weighted averaging, so KV grows O(log n). Pure software, nothing fabricated.
why: Long-context KV becomes O(log n) instead of O(n): a 1M-token context fits in roughly 20k tokens of KV.

title: Transformer prefetcher in CXL controller makes flash act like DRAM
idea: IFR: infinite capacity at DRAM speed via a perfect oracle. Closest: a CXL expander fronting SLC NAND with a 5% DRAM cache runs an on-controller sequence model trained on each tenant's miss stream (page deltas plus PC hints sent over CXL), issuing prefetches 50-100 us ahead.
why: 4-8x less DRAM for graph analytics and recommendation at under 15% slowdown once hit rate exceeds 99%.

title: Minify every pointer to 32 bits with hardware expansion
idea: Minify 64-bit pointers to 32-bit region-relative offsets in a new C/C++ ABI mode. The load/store unit adds a per-region base register on the fly (like Java compressed oops, but for native code), and a trap widens a region if it overflows 4 GB x alignment.
why: Pointer-heavy structures (trees, graphs, ORMs, kernels) shrink 20-45%, which buys ~1.2-1.6x effective capacity with no new silicon process.

title: Post-it note: back-end oxide-TFT metadata layer stuck atop DRAM
idea: A sticky note added after the book is printed: deposit a <=350 C IGZO thin-film-transistor memory layer on top of finished DRAM or controller wafers to hold compression tags, hotness counters and dedup pointers; because metadata is recomputable it needs only seconds of retention and tolerates bit loss.
why: Frees the 3-6% of DRAM bits and the metadata-cache misses that compression/dedup cost; all added steps are back-end compatible (<=400 C) on mature US tools.

title: Sourdough starter: cultured dictionaries recompress cold pages
idea: Like a sourdough culture that is kept alive and fed, idle cores keep a per-workload compression dictionary that is trained continuously on sampled cold pages (zstd-style dictionary learning, refreshed hourly). Cold pages are 'fermented' by re-encoding them with the current culture. Old culture versions are kept so older pages stay decodable.
why: Dictionary-primed compression of 4 KB pages achieves a 1.5-2x better ratio than plain LZ on small blocks, turning a 2x compressed tier into about 3x with no new hardware.

title: Lisp-machine-style hardware GC tracer beside the memory controller
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: burn garbage faster with a 180 nm tracing coprocessor next to memory (like the Symbolics and TI Explorer GC assists) that marks reachable objects in parallel at memory bandwidth using tag bits, so managed runtimes collect continuously and run heaps at ~1.2x live size instead of the usual 2-3x.
why: Java/Go/JS/Python fleets spend 40-60% of heap DRAM on GC headroom; tracing is memory-bound, so old-node logic is fast enough.

title: Dendritic subarrays compute attention scores where the keys live
idea: Neurons integrate synaptic inputs on dendrites before the soma; DRAM subarrays likewise perform bit-serial dot products of a broadcast query against stored keys using charge-sharing logic beside the sense amplifiers, and only top-k indices leave the bank, so no staging copy of the KV cache is needed in HBM.
why: HBM capacity and data movement: removes duplicate KV staging and cuts attention read energy 5-10x.

title: Bubble-memory bootloop maps let partial-capacity HBM stacks ship
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with a bootloop PROM listing bad minor loops, which controllers simply skipped. Apply it to HBM/DDR: instead of scrapping stacks with dead pseudo-channels or subarrays, burn a bootloop map into the base die, sell 20/24/28 GB SKUs, and have the controller and OS remap around dead regions at subarray granularity.
why: Fact 6 (HBM yield down 20-30%): recovering most failing stacks as lower-capacity SKUs raises usable HBM bits per wafer 10-25%.

title: Cored casting: coarse skeleton protected, fine interior repaired by physics
idea: Cored castings are hollow, with metal only where strength is needed. Simulation state is stored as a coarse multigrid level in protected memory plus fine-level residual corrections at 4-8 bits in 1%-BER cells. On each load, a local PDE-residual check flags any cell whose residual jumps (the signature of a bit flip), and only those cells are re-solved from their neighbors and the coarse level.
why: Fine meshes dominate scientific DRAM use; storing them as low-bit residuals cuts footprint 4-8x, and the physics itself detects and corrects errors at 1% BER.

title: Foveated framebuffers stored at eye-tracked resolution
idea: Imposed limit: an AR headset frame may occupy one eighth of its pixel count in DRAM. Eye tracking picks the foveal tile; the display pipeline stores only that tile at full resolution and keeps the periphery as low-resolution mip levels, upsampling in the display controller during scan-out.
why: Framebuffers and render targets dominate XR memory; foveated storage cuts them 4-8x and also saves bandwidth energy.

title: Quorum sensing decides when shared pages get local replicas
idea: Bacteria act only when autoinducer concentration crosses a threshold; each host counts remote accesses to a pooled page from its cores, makes a local replica only when demand crosses a quorum, and dissolves it when the signal decays, otherwise serving the page from the shared CXL pool.
why: Replication overhead: 30-60% fewer duplicate copies of shared data in pooled racks.

title: Consume-on-read: destructive DRAM read becomes free reclaim
idea: Add an RD-CONSUME memory command that reverses DRAM's read-then-restore order: the sense amp delivers the line, skips the restore, and the controller flips the line to 'free' in a bitmap. Queues, NN activations and NIC ring buffers that are read exactly once get their capacity back at read time, with no software free or zeroing.
why: Turns fact 8 (destructive read) into a feature: buffer and activation pools shrink ~20-40% because slots recycle at read time, and each consumed read skips the restore part of activate energy.

title: Content-addressed physical memory: the hash picks the address
idea: Flip address->content into content->address: the controller hashes each 64 B line and stores it in a slot chosen by the hash, with a reference count; page tables map virtual lines to content IDs, so identical lines (zeros, shared libraries, the same weights across tenants) physically exist once.
why: Line-granular dedup with no software scanning; multi-tenant cloud and VM hosts typically gain 1.3-2x effective capacity.

title: Seismic stacking: memory-side reduce-on-write for accumulation buffers
idea: Borrowed from seismic and astronomical co-adding, where traces are summed on arrival instead of stored: memory expanders implement vector add-on-write (FP32/BF16), so N producers (gradient buckets, histograms, embedding-gradient scatters) accumulate into one shared buffer instead of each holding a private copy for a later reduction.
why: Removes N-1 copies of accumulation buffers; 2-8x less DRAM for reduction-heavy workloads.

title: Leitner boxes: spaced-repetition promotion from NV into DRAM
idea: Like flashcards moving up Leitner boxes only after recalls at spaced intervals, pages live in persistent memory by default and are promoted one box at a time (NV -> compressed DRAM -> plain DRAM) only after accesses at increasing intervals, filtering one-off scans.
why: Prevents scan pollution from bloating DRAM tiers; keeps DRAM to the truly recurrent working set, ~20-30% smaller for the same hit rate.

title: Fleet-trained static dictionaries burned into memory-controller firmware
idea: This adds zero masks. A dictionary of the most frequent 64 B patterns (pointers, zero runs, float templates, ELF and JIT idioms) is trained on years of fleet memory dumps and shipped yearly into controller SRAM through firmware. Every line then compresses against fleet-scale statistics instead of local history.
why: 1.3-1.6x extra compression on small lines, where local adaptive codecs fail, so hosts need less installed DRAM.

title: Pollinator robots move memory sleds to where demand blooms
idea: Bees ferry pollen between flowers; rack robots carry blind-mate, hot-plug CXL memory sleds rated for thousands of insertions from underused racks to those whose KV and batch demand will peak, guided by tomorrow's forecast.
why: Utilization: 20-30% less DRAM fleet-wide by moving bits to demand instead of provisioning every rack for its own peak.

title: Neuroscientist's predictive brain: store only prediction residuals in memory controller
idea: The cortex mostly transmits prediction errors. The memory controller runs cheap per-line predictors (stride, delta from the neighboring line, or the previous version of the line) and stores just the residual plus a 2-bit predictor tag. This is video motion compensation applied to arrays, page tables, counters and timestamps.
why: Numeric arrays and pointers are highly predictable. Residual coding gets 2-4x on exactly the data where dictionary and LZ methods fail, raising effective capacity per bit.

title: Trust-domain-salted dedup with constant-time copy-on-write
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: instead of fleet-wide page dedup (switched off after Flip-Feng-Shui and timing side channels), salt dedup fingerprints per trust domain so pages merge only inside one tenant, and route every write to a mergeable page through the same constant-latency CoW path whether shared or not. Each region gets its own dedup policy instead of one global on/off switch.
why: Resolves 'dedup saves memory vs dedup leaks information'; recovers 10-30% capacity on VM/container hosts where dedup is disabled today.

title: Vehicle-to-grid sessions: clients store their own encrypted state
idea: Like EVs lending their batteries to the grid, user devices persist their own compressed, encrypted, MAC-tagged session state (quantized gist/KV tokens, app session) in local flash and upload it with the next request, so servers hold no DRAM for idle users.
why: Idle-user state is the bulk of serving memory; pushes it onto already-paid-for client flash and sizes server DRAM only to active requests.

title: Eliminate per-accelerator weight replicas via optical multicast weight broadcast
idea: Keep one copy of model weights in a pooled memory appliance and broadcast each layer's weights over a passive optical splitter to 8-64 accelerators that consume them in lockstep; local HBM holds only KV and activations.
why: Removes 8-64x duplication of weights across a serving pod; HBM per accelerator could drop 50-70%, easing the HBM TSV-tax bottleneck.

title: Train models with KV-dropout so memory starvation is harmless
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: inject random KV eviction (drop 30-70% of past tokens' KV, biased toward older ones) as a regularizer during pre- and post-training, turning the harm of missing context into learned robustness so inference can evict aggressively with negligible quality loss.
why: KV eviction degrades unadapted models; evictability-trained models could run at 2-4x smaller KV budgets.

title: Attention-mass bit-plane decay for KV entries
idea: The information an entry must keep scales with the attention it receives: an entry with cumulative softmax weight 1e-4 needs only a few bits. Store KV in bit-plane-major layout and, as a per-token running attention-mass counter decays, free the lowest bit planes in place (16 to 8 to 4 to 2 bits), so precision degrades gracefully instead of tokens being evicted.
why: 3-6x KV capacity at near-lossless quality; freeing whole planes needs no rewrite or compaction.

title: Americium credit: U.S. tax credit per gigabyte of DRAM avoided
idea: Named for the Americas, a CHIPS-style federal credit pays data-center operators per GB-year of DRAM avoided against a certified baseline (via compression, pooling, reuse) measured by a standard telemetry audit, and federal procurement favors software that publishes bytes-per-transaction figures.
why: Makes memory efficiency a domestic supply lever while the U.S. makes only 1-2% of DRAM; a 15% demand cut equals several fabs' output without $15B of capital (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: CERN two-level trigger decides which KV entries survive
idea: Borrowed from LHC trigger systems that keep ~1 event in 100,000: new KV entries wait in a fixed-latency level-1 SRAM ring while on-die accumulators sum the attention mass each token receives over the next K steps; only tokens passing the L1 threshold are promoted to DRAM, and a slower software 'high-level trigger' periodically re-scores and drops survivors.
why: Long-context KV grows linearly with tokens; physics-style triggering can keep 5-20% of tokens at small accuracy loss, a 5-20x KV reduction.

title: Airline overbooking: sell 140% of rack DRAM, keep CXL standby seats
idea: Treat DRAM like airline seats: provision each server at ~70% of its tenants' summed peak, size a rack-level CXL pool from no-show statistics, and 'bump' the lowest-value pages (compress first, then pool) when a peak lands; the hypervisor publishes a per-VM bump-probability SLA.
why: Fleets provisioned for sum-of-peaks leave 25-40% of DRAM idle; overbooking math cuts DIMMs purchased 20-30% at a quantified SLA risk.

title: Minify per-variant weights: 1-bit sign deltas over one base
idea: Minify the cost of serving thousands of fine-tuned models by holding one shared base model in HBM plus per-variant 1-bit sign deltas with per-row scales, applied on the fly in the matmul kernel.
why: Each extra variant costs ~16x less memory than a full copy, collapsing the DRAM a multi-tenant fine-tune platform needs.

title: Johnson-noise Morris counters shrink telemetry and tiering tables tenfold
idea: Replace exact 32-bit counters in flow tables, feature-frequency tables and page-hotness tables with 4-bit probabilistic Morris counters. Each one increments with probability 2^-c, decided by a comparator on amplified resistor thermal noise. Johnson noise grows with temperature, so the entropy source improves at 125 C rather than degrading.
why: Counting and telemetry structures in hot edge gateways shrink 8-10x, freeing DRAM.

title: Bicycle gears: bit-plane tiering serves weights at shiftable precision
idea: Store weights transposed into bit-planes: the 4 most-significant planes stay in DRAM/HBM, low planes live in CXL or flash; each request 'shifts gear' by fetching only as many planes as its quality tier needs, and speculative decoding uses MSB-only planes as a free draft model.
why: Cuts DRAM held for weights 2-4x without storing multiple quantized copies; fetch energy scales with precision actually used.

title: Pool memory over polyolefin twinax and acrylate-coated fiber, no FEP
idea: Box: pool × rack interconnect × rack × deployment × foamed PE/PP-insulated twinax + Ge-core silica fiber with urethane-acrylate coating. CXL memory-pooling fabrics are cabled with fluorine-free dielectrics and connectors, and retimers equalize the slightly higher loss so a PFAS ban does not block pooling.
why: Pooling cuts stranded DRAM 10–25% fleetwide, but default high-speed cables use FEP/PTFE; a fluorine-free cable bill of materials keeps that saving deployable.

title: Satellite downlink budgets: storage-side filtering before data reaches DRAM
idea: Borrowed from Earth-observation satellites that process onboard because downlink is scarce: each query gets a 'downlink budget' in host DRAM bytes, and the planner pushes filters, projections and pre-aggregation into computational SSDs until the result fits, so raw scans never land in DRAM.
why: Analytics engines buffer raw columnar data in DRAM; pushing selection into storage cuts working-set DRAM 5-20x for selective queries.

title: Keyword-spotter extreme: ternary weights stored as zero-skipping trit runs
idea: From always-on keyword spotters that run ternary networks: models are trained to {-1, 0, +1} weights stored as base-3 packed trits (5 per byte) with run-length skip lists for zeros, decoded by adder-only compute units that skip zero runs.
why: About 1.6 bits per weight or less versus 16 is a 10x+ cut in weight DRAM/HBM, and fab water falls proportionally.

title: Reuse row-hammer activation counters as free tiering telemetry
idea: Worsen: add yet more counters and page-table scans to find cold memory. Flip: export the per-row activation counts that PRAC/RFM row-hammer defenses already keep inside new DRAM to the OS, which uses them as a zero-overhead hotness map to demote cold rows to a compressed or CXL tier.
why: Capacity: makes aggressive tiering cheap enough to cut local DRAM 30-50% at no telemetry cost; reuses hardware mandated anyway.

title: Idle consumer RAM leased as an erasure-coded remote cache
idea: Worsen: let a billion PCs sit with gigabytes of unused RAM. Flip: a client leases idle consumer RAM to a cloud remote-memory service, striping cache data with erasure codes across many homes so it survives churn, and pays owners per GB-hour.
why: Cost: idle RAM has near-zero marginal cost, giving 100x+ cheaper cache GB; trades latency (ms), privacy engineering and churn.

title: Minify writability: mask-ROM DIMMs for immutable system pages
idea: Minify the writable footprint by moving the kernel text, libc, Python, CUDA libraries and popular container base layers into ultra-dense NOR-style mask-ROM DIMMs mapped read-only at ~50 ns. These are reflashed yearly as 'golden releases'.
why: 5-15% of every server's DRAM holds identical code and read-only data. ROM costs a fraction of DRAM per bit and needs no refresh or EUV.

title: Follow-the-moon placement of memory-hungry jobs across regions
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: route memory-heavy batch work (long-context KV-heavy jobs, analytics, fine-tuning) to whichever regions are in their nightly interactive trough, so each region's DRAM is sized for the global average instead of its own daytime peak plus batch.
why: Diurnal peak-to-trough ratios of 2-3x mean 20-35% less global DRAM; needs only schedulers and existing networks.

title: Phase-shifting jobs to anticorrelate memory peaks in a pool
idea: Provisioning for the sum of peaks instead of the peak of the sum wastes capacity. A scheduler fingerprints each job's memory-over-time curve (batch ETL, training checkpoints, nightly builds) and offsets start times so that peaks interleave, then sizes the shared pool to the measured peak of the sum plus a margin.
why: In mixed fleets the peak of the sum is typically 30-50% below the sum of peaks, and pool DRAM falls by about as much.

title: Stained glass from shards: salvaged DRAM dies become CXL expanders
idea: Artists turn shards into windows: desolder DRAM packages from decommissioned servers (reflow <260 C), retest and bin them, and remount them on low-temperature panel-level substrates behind a compressing CXL controller, producing new capacity-tier modules from e-waste.
why: Millions of DDR4 DIMMs retire yearly; reuse adds supply at near-zero wafer cost and no high-temperature step, and compression makes old density competitive (~2x effective).

title: Double-entry ledgers: derive state from an append-only NVM journal
idea: Borrowed from accounting, where balances are derived from an immutable journal: services keep only an append-only event log in non-volatile memory and compute derived views (indexes, aggregates, session state) on demand into SRAM scratch, caching only results whose reuse distance is under a millisecond.
why: Eliminates large DRAM-resident materialized views and session caches in transactional systems; no long-lived volatile state, so zero refresh power.

title: Export idle host DRAM of GPU servers as far memory
idea: Inverts 'a server's DRAM serves only its own CPU': GPU servers carry 1-2 TB of host DRAM that sits mostly idle while the GPUs work from HBM. An RDMA far-memory daemon leases those idle bytes to neighboring CPU servers for swap and tiering over existing NICs.
why: Unlocks 30-60% of host DRAM in AI racks for the rest of the fleet with no new chips.

title: Per-block local losses discard activations before next block runs
idea: Reverse the training order from forward-all-then-backward-all to forward-and-learn per block: each block gets an auxiliary head or a forward-gradient estimate, updates at once, and frees its activations before the next block executes.
why: Stored activations are often 60-80% of training memory; per-block learning makes them O(1 block) instead of O(depth), a 10-50x cut in activation memory if accuracy holds.

title: Local-loss training lets each block free activations immediately
idea: Inverts 'backprop must store every activation': blocks train on local objectives (per-block predictive or contrastive heads, plus a periodic short global sync), so each block's activations are freed as soon as its local update finishes.
why: Activation memory, often 50-80% of the training footprint at long sequence lengths, shrinks to about one block's worth: a 10-30x cut in activation memory.

title: Rack-level content-addressed line store for shared weights
idea: Worsen: every tenant on every host holds its own copy of the same model weights and runtimes. Flip: a CXL memory appliance hashes each 4 KB block on write and stores it once in a content-addressed table; hosts map their pages to the hash, and copy-on-write breaks sharing only on mutation.
why: Capacity: 5-20x less DRAM for replicated read-mostly data (weights, libraries, VM images) across a rack.

title: Tin pest: KV entries crumble to lower precision with age
idea: White tin crumbles to grey powder after long cold exposure; each KV block carries an age counter and a background engine requantizes old tokens fp16 to int8 to int4 to int2, keeping ~1% attention-sink and high-score tokens at full precision, on a per-layer schedule set by measured attention entropy.
why: Older tokens get little attention mass, so average KV bits per token fall 4-6x on 100k+ contexts and one GPU holds several times more context (density).

title: Roll-to-roll assembled memory ribbons with a compressor per die
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): flexible-hybrid-electronics lines place thinned DRAM dies and tiny compression/decompression chiplets alternately on a printed-interconnect flex ribbon, so every DRAM die gets its own inline compressor, and the ribbon is sold by effective (compressed) GB.
why: Inline compression per die at negligible board cost gives ~2x effective capacity, while roll-to-roll assembly lowers module cost and avoids rigid-substrate bottlenecks.

title: Value-stream map: classify every resident byte into the seven wastes
idea: Lean value-stream mapping, applied to memory. An always-on profiler (page access bits, allocator tags, PEBS sampling) assigns every resident byte to one of Toyota's wastes: overproduction (prefetched, never used), inventory (cold for over 10 min), defects (leaked), overprocessing (duplicate copies or serializations) and waiting (pinned buffers). It then outputs a ranked kaizen list with automatic fixes such as madvise, compression, dedup and buffer shrinking.
why: Fleet studies often find 20-50% of DRAM cold or wasted; systematic waste accounting can recover about 25% of capacity without hardware changes.

title: Lithium intercalation allocator: tiny objects packed into size-class slack
idea: As Li+ ions slot into the gaps between graphite layers, the allocator intercalates sub-64 B objects into the unused tail slack of larger size-class slots (a 300 B object in a 384 B slot leaves 84 B), tracking them with a per-slab slack bitmap and CHERI-style bounded pointers so overflows trap instead of corrupting neighbors.
why: Size-class internal fragmentation wastes ~10-20% of heap in jemalloc/tcmalloc fleets; reclaiming the slack gives ~8-15% less DRAM with no new memory hardware (cost/bit, density).

title: Lumber grading: bit-planes sorted into clear-grade and framing-grade memory
idea: Sawmills grade boards: clear wood for visible faces, knotty #3 for hidden studs. Tensors are stored as bit-planes. The sign and top two magnitude planes go to strongly coded memory, and the lower planes go raw into 1%-BER cells. The plane boundary is chosen per tensor so that the expected flip error (2^k x 1%) stays below the quantization noise.
why: 60-75% of each number's bits are low-significance planes where 1% flips add noise below the quantization floor, so high-grade memory demand falls 3-4x.
